Two jobs. On the title, the raster interrupt at $A801 uses it as the ticker's fine-scroll countdown. In play, the input scan at $3791 clears it on every call, and the player states read it at $1091, $14C6 and $1AD5, where $FE would turn Willy round on the spot. The only store of $FE, at $3834, sits behind a test that $60 can never pass (see $0060), so in play it is always $00.

Meant to hold the last horizontal direction, so that $3791 can spot a reversal: $49 XOR $60 is $FE only when one is $FF and the other $01. Nothing sets it before play, and the one store to it, at $3838, is inside that same test, so it stays $00, the test never passes and the turn-round at $1091 never happens.

Bytes from $05C6 to $07F7, which nothing in the game reads or writes: the rest of the 1000-byte screen at $0400, to $07E7, still holding spaces, and the 16 bytes after it, $07E8-$07F7, which hold the power-on pattern. The game never shows this screen in play.

The sprite pointers that go with the screen at $0400, which only the code card at $3A02 shows; it points its sprites at $28-$2C, the shapes at $0A00-$0B3F. Play uses the screen at $7C00 and its pointers at $7FF8.

The gameplay keyboard scan at $37C3 stores the eight rows of the keyboard matrix here, $0800-$0807, one byte per row. In the file as loaded, $0800 is the zero byte BASIC needs before a program, and the BCS crackers' BASIC line starts at $0801; the first scan in play overwrites both.

The BCS crackers' one-line BASIC program, 10 SYS2061: link $080B, line number 10, the SYS token $9E and "2061", the zero that ends the line at $080A, then the two zero bytes at $080B that end the program. SYS 2061 runs the start-up at $080D. In play, $0801-$0807 hold rows two to eight of the keyboard matrix (see $0800).

The BCS crackers' start-up, run once by SYS 2061: stores $CBE5 at $033C/$033D, which nothing reads, sets the processor port to $36 (BASIC ROM out, KERNAL and I/O in) and jumps to the title at $A000. It replaces the original loader's way in, which ran the code card at $3A02 first.

34 bytes of code nothing runs, $081E-$083F, after the start-up's last instruction, the JMP $A000 whose last byte is here at $081D. They hold the end of a store to $01, a short delay loop, copies of the interrupt vector $0314/$0315 into $08A0-$08A3, and LDA #$00 with the first byte of a store that the room copy at $0840 cuts off. They are what was in memory here when the file was saved, from an earlier loader.
Current room work copy. $2E55 exposes all RAM with $01=$34, copies one canonical room page here, then restores $01=$36.
Up to seven guardian records for the current room, eight bytes each, copied from the guardian table at $2443 when Willy enters a room.
Guardian records 2 to 7 of the current room, $0948-$0977, eight bytes each; the first record is at $0940.
Eight bytes after the seventh guardian record, not used by the game. The guardians' direction and frame state follows at $0980, their moving coordinates at $0988.
Seven bytes of current guardian direction/animation state.
Seven bytes of current guardian moving coordinates.
The code card's empty-slot marker, sprite pointer $28 in VIC bank 0: a shape like a chess pawn. $3B20 shows it in all four colour slots before a key is pressed.
The code card's keycap for key 1, sprite pointer $29: a raised key with a 1 on it. Pressing 1 on the code card shows it, in red, in the current slot.
The code card's keycap for key 2, sprite pointer $2A, shown in green.
The code card's keycap for key 3, sprite pointer $2B, shown in blue.
The code card's keycap for key 4, sprite pointer $2C, shown in yellow.
$F4, the byte before the leftover editor's command loop at $0B41. What it was for is unknown.

The first surviving instruction of a text-buffer editor that was in memory when the game was saved, and is loaded with it: nothing in the game calls it. It keeps a command line at $0100, reads an optional decimal repeat count, dispatches the commands @ to Z through the table at $0C60, and keeps its buffer pointers in $5D/$5E and $5F/$60. Part of it lay below here: it jumps to $0912 and $0915 and its K command is at $090C, all now in the current room's copy at $0840-$093F. $10CB and several command routines from $101F up are now the game's own code, so it could not run as it stands.

Resets the stack pointer to $FF, the command index $65 and the copy flag $6A, reads the repeat count, dispatches the command through a trampoline at $74 and repeats it while $6F is not zero. It leaves to $0912, part of the editor that is no longer here.

Saves Y in $6E, reads the next command character through $0B8E, then loads Y back from $6E, keeping the flags $0B8E left (PHP/PLP). Only Y is put back: the command index $65 stays moved on. Nothing in the surviving code calls it.

Reads $0100,Y using the index $65, moves the index on and compares the character with the terminator, byte 1. An index of 40 or more branches to the overflow path at $0BAC, which clears the command line and sets the status CO.
Clears the command line through $0EAC, then stores byte 1 through $0BA1. The line buffer is 40 bytes long.
Stores A at $0100 plus index $65, increments the index and returns through $0C1B while within the 40-byte buffer. Overflow follows the CO status path.
Clears the command buffer and puts the status letters CO in $6B/$6C; the routine at $10CB that showed them has been overwritten by the game.
Puts the status letters E? in $6B/$6C. The status path calls $10CB and returns to $0915, neither of which holds editor code in this file.

Skips byte-1 spaces and parses ASCII decimal digits, multiplying the repeat accumulator $6F by ten. Limits the result to one byte; an omitted/zero repeat becomes one. The first non-digit is kept in $62 for command dispatch.
Initializes lower buffer pointer $5D/$5E and upper pointer $5F/$60 from X and boundary high bytes $7E/$7F.
Sets CR when copy mode $6A is nonzero, otherwise OK, in status bytes $6B/$6C.
Decrements X, stores it in copy flag $6A and returns.
32 little-endian addresses of editor routines. Some point at the editing helpers that survive here, others at code the game has overwritten. Nothing in the surviving fragment reads this table.

27 little-endian addresses of editor commands, chosen by the command character minus $40, so @ to Z. H is hex insertion ($0D46), I literal insertion ($0D34) and S search ($0E0B). Several point at code that is no longer the editor's.
AND #$7F precedes the X=0 store entry at $0C98. This clears the high bit of an inserted byte.

Sets X=0, compares current pointer $5D/$5E with limit $5F/$60, writes A through ($5D,X) if space remains, optionally updates copy tracking and advances the current pointer. Controlled literal and hex calls matched output bytes and pointer increments.

Four short trampolines, each choosing by the N flag between two opposite operations: $0CBE between dropping the byte before the gap ($0CDE) and the byte after it ($0D21); $0CC6 between moving one byte forward ($0DC3) and back ($0DA1); $0CCE between moving forward past the next return ($0DE6) and back to the start of the line ($0DB5); $0CD6 between going to the start ($0D8B) and to the end ($0D9A) of the text. Only the table at $0C20 points at them.
Moves pointer $5D/$5E backward unless it is at the lower page boundary $7E. In copy mode, copies the encountered byte through $66/$67. Returns carry clear after a move.

Steps $5D/$5E back with $0CDE once without testing, then again until the byte at $5D is $0D (a carriage return) or the lower bound stops it with carry set. On a return it goes to $0CAF, which in copy mode takes the return back off the copy buffer ($0E7D) and moves $5D/$5E forward one byte, so the pointer ends just after the return, carry clear. $5F/$60 does not move, so the bytes passed leave the text: it deletes back to the start of the line.

Part of the text editor saved with the game. Deletes the text up to and including the next return: it calls $0D21, which copies a byte from ($5F) to ($5D), moves both on and then steps $5D/$5E back ($0CDE), so only $5F/$60 advances; it stops when carry is set or the byte was $0D.
Calls forward transfer $0DC3, saves its byte, moves the current pointer backward again and restores the saved byte and clear carry on success.
Reads command-buffer characters through $0B8E and stores them through $0C9A until byte 1 terminates the text. A controlled call inserted HELLO exactly and advanced $5D/$5E by five.

Reads two hexadecimal characters, shifts the first nibble four bits, ORs in the second and stores the resulting byte through $0C98. Controlled inputs 00, 12, 4A and FF produced the matching bytes and one-byte pointer advances.
Turns an ASCII digit or A-F into its value 0-15. For a letter it adds 8 with the carry still set by the comparison, then masks with $0F. Anything else jumps to the error path.

Reads one command character through $0B8E. Byte 1 and any character below ASCII 0 ($30) are rejected through $0D6B (TXA; JMP $0BB9), the editor error path. A digit 0-9 comes back as its value with carry clear; a character from $3A up comes back unchanged with carry set, for the hex helper. The repeat parser at $0BC5 is the separate routine that skips byte-1 spaces.
The @ command: reads one decimal digit through $0D6F, rejects anything else or a zero, and stores the value 1-9 in $56. What the setting controlled is unknown.
Moves backward, decrements upper pointer $5F/$60 and transfers a byte from ($5D,X) to ($5F,X). X is zero on the command-dispatch route.

Sets X=0 and transfers one byte backward with $0DA1 without testing, then keeps transferring backward until carry is set (the lower bound) or the byte moved is $0D. At the lower bound it returns with carry set. On a $0D it falls into the forward helper at $0DC1, which moves the return forward again, so the pointers end just after the previous return.
Sets X=0, reads through upper pointer $5F/$60, writes through current pointer $5D/$5E and increments both pointers. Boundary high byte $7F limits the transfer.

Repeats $0DC3 until the byte it moved is $0D or $0DC3 returns carry set. Carry is set at the upper bound, and also in copy mode when $0E7D finds the copy pointer at its base: it then turns copy mode off and the move stops.
Sets $63 to $11, toggles bits 3-6 of $6D (EOR with the constant $78), and halves $63 to $08 when bit 6 of the new $6D is set. What the flags controlled is unknown.
Toggles bit 7 of the editor's flag byte $64 and returns.

Searches from upper buffer pointer $5F/$60 for the command-buffer pattern starting at $0100+$65, terminated by byte 1. Uses temporary pointer $5B/$5C and moves the gap/buffer pointers forward to the end of a match. Failure follows the S status path.
Sets copy pointer $66/$67 from X and boundary page $7C, then writes X into copy flag $6A.
Decrements copy pointer $66/$67 unless it is at low byte zero and lower-bound page $7C.
Copies backward from the saved copy pointer through temporary $68/$69, storing bytes via $0C9A until the page-bound or store-bound condition stops it.
Writes 40 dot bytes ($2E) to $0100-$0127, then clears command index $65.
Calls forward transfer $0DC1; if its boundary condition sets carry, returns substitute byte $1A. Clears carry before returning.

The editor's initialiser: clears $74, the first byte of the trampoline that $0B6E calls (its address goes in $75/$76), sets $56, the setting the @ command changes, to 9, writes RTS ($60) at $B000, copies eight settings from $0EDC to $78-$7F and jumps to $0810. In this file $B000 is the first byte of room 0's record and $0810 falls inside the BCS start-up, at the second byte of its STA $033C at $080F, so it would wreck the game if called; nothing calls it.

Eight settings the initialiser at $0EC2 copies to $78-$7F: 00 13 ED 27 50 54 54 B0. The last four are page bounds the surviving routines use: $7C ($50) is the copy buffer's base ($0E74, $0E7D, $0E8D), $7D ($54) the page the copy pointer may not reach ($0CF2), $7E ($54) the text's lower bound ($0BFA, $0CDE) and $7F ($B0) its upper bound ($0BFA, $0DC3, $0E0B). Nothing that survives reads $78-$7B, and what they meant is unknown.
Saves X at $53, calls KERNAL GETIN ($FFE4), restores X and loads Y from $52 while preserving the returned flags.
The start of a routine that works on colour memory: it saves X, points $84/$85 at $D800 and reads $81. It stops after LDA #$DB at $0EFF, cut off by the fill at $0F01.
Fill after the cut-off editor routine, in runs of $FF and $00: 31 bytes of $FF from $0F01 to $0F1F, 32 zero bytes to $0F3F, 32 bytes of $FF to $0F5F and 32 zero bytes to $0F7F.
Thirty-two bytes before the restart stub at $0FA0: $70, then 31 bytes of $FF. The meaning of the $70 is unknown.

Restart stub: reads the processor port $01, clears bit 0 (LORAM, which takes BASIC ROM out) and jumps to the title at $A000. That works after RESTORE, while $00 still makes bit 0 an output; after a reset $00 is 0, the write changes nothing and the jump lands in BASIC ROM. The code card jumps here at $3C4B after a correct code, and the success header it copies to $8000 points both cartridge vectors here. In this release neither happens: the code card never runs, and the header at $8000 is the failure one, with a broken signature.
Sends a move to the right on by player state: in a jump (state 1) to $1372, which carries the jump one step right; in any other state out through $1021, the rest of the main loop.
Eight bytes between the two collision trampolines that nothing reaches.
Sends a move to the left on by player state: in a jump (state 1) to $1414, which carries the jump one step left; in any other state out through $1021, the rest of the main loop.
Padding before the player tick entry at $1000.
The entry to one player update: a jump to $1075. $3349 comes here once the stack is reset.
State 0's handler, $1091, the first of the seven words at $1003-$1010 that $107E indexes by twice the player's state $33.
High byte $10 of the first little-endian word at $1003 (JSW_State_player_state_dispatch_table); the parent description defines the table or writable pointer.
The handlers of states 1-6 in the table at $1003: $123D jumping, $11FB falling, $14C1 on a ramp, $151F carried by a conveyor, $1538 just onto a conveyor, $1ABC holding a rope.
Writable indirect player-state target loaded from the dispatch table before JMP ($1011).
High byte $10 of the first little-endian word at $1011 (JSW_State_current_player_handler); the parent description defines the table or writable pointer.

The signed horizontal direction of a jump, set when the jump starts: from $49 at $10B4, from the conveyor's direction $13 at $1529 when Willy jumps off a conveyor, and at $15A8, $15DF and $1B22. The scrap of source at $9A80 calls it JPDIR.
Temporary X cell used by the collision probes.
Player state saved on entry to conveyor-contact state 5.
First-pass flag for conveyor-contact state 5.

The way Willy was going as he came onto a conveyor: $01 right, $FF left or 0 neither. Player state 5 works it out on its first pass ($1557, $1564, $1572) and is the only reader ($1575, $1583, $15E5); state 4 uses the conveyor's direction $13 instead.
Rope animation divider.
Rope trajectory/segment index used by attached state 6.
Attached-to-rope movement divider.
Tail-calls the current input scanner through the vector at $CFF0, which play sets to $3791.

JMP ($CFF2), which $2D48 sets to $3349: the stack is reset and the player update runs again from $1000. A state handler jumps here after changing the state in $33, so the new state's handler runs at once.

JMP ($CFF4), which $2D52 sets to $334F: the rest of the main loop after the player update, which resets the stack, plays the item sound when the count has changed and goes on to the sprite collisions at $3392.
JMP ($CFF6), which $2D5C sets to $35E4, the tile lookup: the kind of tile in the cell at column X and row Y, in A.
JMP ($CFF8), which $2D66 sets to $2DC6: Willy is placed at the edge of the room he enters by and the room in $0E is built.
JMP ($CFFA), which $2D70 sets to $38EF, the death sequence.

The jump's 36 vertical steps, $102D-$1050, one added to Willy's height $1C on each update of a jump ($1257 reads it by the index $52): rising in steps of 2 and 1 pixels, level at the top, then falling by 1 and 2. This byte is step 0, which is 0.
Steps 1-35 of the jump table at $102D.
The kind of tile one cell right of the probe column $1014, in row $0F, through $1024.
The kind of tile at the probe column $1014 and row $0F, through $1024.
The kind of tile at the probe column $1014, one row above $0F, through $1024.
The kind of tile at the probe column $1014, two rows below $0F, through $1024: the cell under Willy's feet, Willy being two cells tall.
The start of every player update: the room-select cheat ($1BBC, switched off by its RTS), then $1C4C, which catches Willy on a rope, then on through $107B.

Calls $16A2, which in a room with a rope moves the rope on and stages its sprites every second call, then runs the handler for the player's state at $107E. The rope code jumps here too, from $1B0B and $1BB0, after it changes the state.
Runs the handler for the player's state: $33, 0 to 6, picks a word of the table at $1003, which goes to $1011 for the JMP ($1011). Nothing checks that $33 is in range.

Player state 0, standing or walking. When $4B is $FE it turns Willy round on the spot, flipping bit 2 of the frame $50; $4B is never $FE in play (see $004B). Otherwise it trims Willy's height $1C to a whole cell. A jump request ($4A) starts state 1, with the jump's direction $1013 taken from $49 and the counters $52 and $51 cleared, and runs it through $101E; with no direction it leaves through $1021, and a direction goes on to $10C7.

Walks right ($10CC) when the value just loaded is positive or zero, and left ($112A) when it is negative. $10C2 comes here with the direction $49, and the conveyor's state 4 at $1535 with the conveyor's direction $13.

One step of a walk to the right. Willy's place across a cell is a phase $32, 0 to 7. From phase 2 the phase counts up, with the frame $50 at half of it, and at 8 he moves into the next cell at phase 0, where $106B and $11B1 test the cell under his feet. At phase 0 or 1 he is at the cell's edge: in column $1F that is the room's right exit, which takes the room from $20, starts the fall state 2 and builds the room through $1027; elsewhere $1187 handles the two cells ahead and $11C4 the one under them, and the phase becomes 2.

One step of a walk to the left, the mirror of $10CC. In column 0 at phase 0 Willy takes the room's left exit ($1F). At phase 6 or 7, $1187 handles the two cells of his own column and $11C4 the one under them, and the phase becomes 5; otherwise the phase counts down, with the frame $50 at half of it plus 4 (facing left), and below 0 he moves into the cell to the left at phase 7, where $106B and $11B1 test the cell under his feet.

Handles a cell Willy walks into, by its kind in A: a wall (2) stops him, leaving through $1021; a ramp (4) puts him in state 3 through $1695 and $101E, unless his direction $49 is the ramp's direction $11; a hazard (3) kills him ($15F0); an item (6) is taken ($15FB). Anything else returns. $11B1, after it, starts a fall (state 2, with $51 cleared) when the cell under Willy's feet in a new cell is air (0) or an item (6).

Handles the cell under Willy's feet, by its kind in A: a conveyor (5) puts him in state 5, saving his state in $1015 and clearing $1016, unless he is in state 4 or 5 already; a hazard (3) kills him ($15F0). Anything else returns. It starts with 18 NOPs.

Player state 2, falling. Willy drops 2 pixels an update, and $51 counts the updates. Each time his height $1C reaches a whole cell: at row 14 he leaves by the room's lower exit ($1E, then $1027); otherwise a count of 17 or more marks the fall as deadly ($53 = $FF), and $12E9 looks for something to land on. If he lands he dies when the fall was deadly, and the fall goes on when he does not.
Player state 1, jumping: moves Willy by the vertical step for this point of the jump from the table at $102D, sideways in the direction at $1013, and probes the tiles he moves into.

Looks for a ceiling as Willy rises in a jump: the cells above his head, through $1062, each handled by $12CB. Which cells, his own column, the next or both, depends on his facing ($50) and phase ($32).

Handles a cell above Willy's head in a jump, by its kind in A: a wall (2) ends the jump and starts a fall (state 2, with the jump index $52 cleared), leaving through $1021; a hazard (3) kills him ($15F0); an item (6) is taken ($15FB). Anything else returns.

Looks for a floor as Willy comes down in a jump or a fall: the cells under his feet, through $106B, each handled by $1321. Which cells, his own column, the next or both, depends on his facing ($50) and phase ($32).

Handles a cell under Willy's feet as he comes down, by its kind in A: floor (1) or wall (2) lands him (state 0); a hazard (3) kills him ($15F0); an item (6) is taken ($15FB); a ramp (4) puts him in state 3, with $1695 setting his phase unless he is in column $1F; a conveyor (5) puts him in state 5, saving his state in $1015 and clearing $1016. Air (0) returns.

Player state 1 jumping to the right, entered from $1247. When the step at the jump index $52 moves Willy and bits 1 and 2 of his height $1C are clear (AND #$06, so at a whole cell or one pixel below one), $13E2 runs first: within two pixels of the top Willy leaves by the room's upper exit ($1D, through $1027), and otherwise $1296 looks for a ceiling in the first 18 steps and $12E9 for a floor after them. Then $1372 takes the step: straight after the ceiling check, unless a wall there has ended the jump, and after the floor check through $0FD2, only while he is still jumping (state 1); a landing leaves through $1021 without the step.

Takes one step of a jump to the right: adds the jump table's step ($102D) to Willy's height $1C and moves him a phase right, with the frame $50 at half the phase. At phase 0 he is at a cell's edge: in column $1F he leaves by the room's right exit ($20, through $1027); elsewhere $14A9 handles the cells ahead, two, or three when bits 1 and 2 of his height are not both clear (AND #$06: a height one pixel below a whole cell still gets two), and the phase becomes 1. At 8 he moves into the next cell at phase 0. Then on to $138F.
Counts the jump on: after the 36th step ($52 reaches $24) the jump ends, with $52 and the fall counter $51 cleared and Willy falling (state 2). Leaves through $1021.

Player state 1 jumping to the left, entered from $1242: the mirror of $1362, with $1487 for the checks when bits 1 and 2 of the height $1C are clear (a whole cell or one pixel below one) and $1414 taking the step. After the floor check $0FE6 goes on to $1414 only while Willy is still jumping (state 1), and otherwise leaves through $1021.

Takes one step of a jump to the left, the mirror of $1372: in column 0 at phase 0 Willy leaves by the room's left exit ($1F); at phase 6 or 7, $14A9 handles the cells of his own column, two or three, and the phase becomes 5; otherwise the phase counts down, and below 0 he moves into the cell to the left at phase 7. The jump is counted on at $1444 as at $138F.

Handles a cell beside Willy in a jump, by its kind in A: a hazard (3) kills him ($15F0); an item (6) is taken ($15FB); a wall (2) stops the step sideways, going straight to $138F, which counts the jump on and leaves. Anything else returns. Jumps both ways use it.
Writable ramp traversal counter used by player state 3.

Player state 3, on a ramp: lifts Willy one cell, two pixels an update for four updates, with the counter at $14C0 going from 8 down by 2, then puts him back in state 0, which walks him on. A climb starts only when the direction held ($49) is against the ramp's stored direction ($11) and his phase $32 is 2 facing right or 6 facing left; otherwise state 0 comes back at once. A height that is 0 once trimmed to a whole cell takes him out by the room's upper exit ($1D). When $4B is not zero it only turns him round. It does not move him across, calls no tile probe and uses only A.

While a climb is under way (the counter $14C0 not zero) this goes straight to $1510, which raises Willy two more pixels; the direction held and his phase are tested only when a climb starts. Player state 3 as a whole climbs one cell, two pixels an update for four updates, then returns to state 0; a climb starts only when the direction held is against the stored ramp direction $11 and the phase is 2 facing right or 6 facing left, and otherwise state 0 comes back at once.
Player state 4, carried by a conveyor: a jump request starts a jump (state 1) in the conveyor's direction $13, with the index $52 cleared; otherwise Willy walks the conveyor's way, through $10C7.
Player state 4 is conveyor-driven grounded movement: the signed room conveyor direction replaces manual horizontal motion, while a jump request enters the normal jump state.

Player state 5, just onto a conveyor. On the first pass ($1016 zero) it trims Willy's height $1C to a whole cell and works out which way he was going, in $1017, from the state saved in $1015: from his facing when it is 0, from the jump's direction $1013 when it is 1, and for any other saved state from $1013 when the fall counter $51 is below 2 and no way otherwise. The saved state is $33 as it was when the conveyor cell was handled: 0 when he walked on ($11C4); on a landing ($1321), the jumping or falling state only when the conveyor cell was the only cell under him that counted, since a landing across two conveyor cells saves 5, from the second cell, and a floor or wall cell handled first saves 0. A jump from a conveyor does not clear $51. Going the conveyor's way ($13), he is carried (state 4). Going no way, he is carried if he faces the conveyor's way; facing against it, a jump goes straight up, holding the direction against it keeps him standing, and anything else lets it carry him. Going against it, holding the direction against it lets him jump that way or walk on against it ($112A or $10CC), and anything else lets it carry him.

On passes after the first ($1016 not zero) this goes straight to $1575. Player state 5 as a whole: the direction worked out on the first pass ($1017), Willy's facing and what is held ($49, $4A) decide whether he is carried (state 4), jumps (state 1), stands still, or walks against the conveyor through $10CC or $112A. He stays in state 5 in the last two; state 5 never puts him back in state 0.
Kills Willy: clears the fall counter $51 and the deadly-fall flag $53 and goes to the death sequence through $102A.
Low byte of the candidate screen address, copied from zero-page $07 by $1609/$160B. Compared against each item cell address at $162D/$162F. This is an address byte, not an X coordinate.
High byte of the candidate screen address, copied from zero-page $08 by $160E/$1610. Compared against each item cell address at $1634/$1636. It is not an input Y coordinate.

Takes the item in the cell the last lookup read, if there is one there: $07/$08 holds that cell's screen address. Each of the 80 item records ($22C3, through $CFFC) in this room ($0E) and not yet taken (byte 3 zero) is looked up by $1024; the one at the same address is marked taken ($FF), its cell becomes air ($20), and the count $0401 goes up by one in decimal, with interrupts off. A count of $50 sets $0400, which sends Maria away. Every call then prints the count's two digits at $7F31 and $7F32.
Sets the probe column $1014 to Willy's cell $4F and the probe row $0F to the row of the top of his sprite, his height $1C divided by 8.
Sets Willy's phase $32 as he steps onto a ramp: 2 when he faces right (frame $50 below 4), 6 when he faces left.

In a room with a rope ($0402), every second call ($1018): copies the three rope sprites for the swing position $0403, from the address the table at $1856 gives, to $0500-$05BF, and their six places, from $178A plus six times the position, to $05C0-$05C5, then clears $0407 so the interrupt at $3538 copies them in. It also turns sprites 5-7 on ($D015) and clears their top X bits ($D010). Then it moves the swing on: positions 0-16 are one half of the swing and 17-33 the other, mirrored, and the position counts by $0406, turning at the ends. In a room without a rope it only resets $1018.
Position 0's places, the first of 34 at $178A-$1855, six bytes each: x and height for rope sprites 5, 6 and 7, which $16A2 stages at $05C0.
Positions 1-33 of the rope's sprite places at $178A, six bytes each: x and height for sprites 5, 6 and 7, which $16A2 stages at $05C0.

The low byte, $00, of pointer 0 ($8100) in the rope's table of 34 little-endian pointers at $1856-$1899, one for each swing position: pointer i is the three rope sprites of position i, which $16A2 copies to $0500. After the pointers come an unused word at $189A and, from $189C, the 17 windows of rope points that $1C86 picks, for player state 6 ($1B62) and for catching Willy on the rope ($1C4C).
High byte $81 of pointer 0 ($8100) in the rope table at $1856. $16D2 reads the table's high bytes as $1857,X, X being twice the swing position $0403.

Pointers 1-33 of the rope table at $1856: pointer i is $8100 + 192 i, the three sprites of swing position i, read at $16CD and $16D2 by twice the position $0403. The word after them, $189A, is $9A80, where a 35th position would start; nothing reads it. From $189C come the 17 windows of $1C86, 32 bytes each, which end where player state 6's code starts, at $1ABC.

Player state 6, holding a rope. $0405 is the way the rope is swinging. Only every second update ($101A) does anything more than place him. On those, a turn on the spot ($4B = $FE, which never happens: see $382C) would turn him round and clear $49 instead of moving him, and still go on to the cell check at $1B37; otherwise Willy moves along the rope, in the index $1019, 0 at the top: holding the direction the rope swings moves him down it, and the other direction up it. Past the bottom (16) he lets go and falls (state 2); past the top he leaves by the room's upper exit ($1D); a jump request jumps off in the direction held (state 1). Still holding on, when his sprite touches a cell's pixels ($D01F), $1B96 looks at the cells around him, and lets him go. An update that leaves him on the rope ends by placing him on it: his x and height come from the window $1C86 picks, the x mirrored as $F7 - x on the second half of the swing (positions 17-33), and his cell, phase and frame from the x.

Meant to handle a cell Willy touches on a rope: a hazard (3) to kill him, air (0) to be passed over, anything else to make him let go. It compares the screen code itself, read through $07/$08 at offset Y, and no room cell's code is 0 or 3 (they are $20-$26), so the first cell it looks at makes him let go and fall (state 2), whatever it holds, and a hazard never kills him there. $1B37 calls it for six cells, two across and three down from his top cell, only when $D01F says his sprite has touched a cell's pixels.

$1BB4 holds the tens of the room number while the room-select cheat at $1BBC waits for its second digit; $1BB5-$1BB9 are the letters it checks, ASCII "FACES"; $1BBA-$1BBB are CLI and RTS, its way out.

A room-select cheat, switched off with a single byte: $60, RTS, stands where the routine's first instruction began, so it returns at once. It is called on every player tick. With its first byte back as $A5 (LDA $43), it waits for ↑ alone, mutes the sound and turns interrupts off, then wants F, A, C, E and S, each typed on its own; a wrong letter leaves. The border turns white, and two digits give a room: the first, 0 to 5, picks the tens from $1C46, the second 0 to 9 the units. It then moves Willy to that room through $1027. It writes the saved border colour to $D014 instead of $D020, but the room build sets the border anyway. Checked live: ↑ FACES 5 7 took Willy to room 57, The Beach.
The rest of the room-select cheat at $1BBC, unreached while its first byte is RTS: $1BBD is the operand $43 of LDA $43. Its tens table, 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, is at $1C46.

Catches Willy on a rope: in a room with one ($0402), when $D01E says his sprite has touched one of the rope's (sprites 5-7) and he is not holding it already, he takes hold (state 6) at the lowest point of the rope at or above his height $1C, which goes to $1019. Reading $D01E clears it.

Points $07/$08 at the rope's 32-byte window for the swing position: $189C plus 32 times the position $0403, less 17 on the second half. A window holds 16 pairs of x and height, from the top of the rope down.

Bytes nothing in the game reads or runs, $1CAE-$1FFF: no instruction or table refers to any of them. $1F00-$1F22 is a routine nothing calls, which copies $C000-$CFFF to $1000-$1FFF, like the one at $AB80; what the rest once was is unknown, and it matches nothing else in memory.
A jump to the initialiser at $2C57. The title program starts a game here.
Two-byte separator before the in-game music initializer.

Starts the in-game tune: points voice 1 at $9C00 and voice 2 at $9DEE and the note table at $20EC, then stores A into $D401-$D418 to clear the SID. In this release A is 1 ($2020), where another crack of the game has 0, so $D415-$D417 are left at 1: the filter takes voice 1 and has no mode selected, and voice 1 plays almost silent for the whole game, since nothing else writes those registers. Then sets both voices' envelopes and pulse widths, gates them with the pulse waveform and sets the volume to 12. Voice 1's end marker jumps back here, so the tune loops.

One tick of the in-game tune, called three times every second frame from $3435 while the music is on ($35). Each voice counts its note down ($94, $95) and reads its next one when the count runs out: voice 1 through $2075, voice 2 through $20B2.

Reads voice 1's next note, a pair of bytes at $90/$91: the pitch, then the length in ticks. A length of $FF is the end of the tune: the return address is dropped and $2005 starts the tune again. Pitch 0 is a rest, which only closes the gate ($20E6). Any other pitch is looked up in the note table at $20EC and the gate opened with pulse waveform ($41). A length of 0 counts as 256, since $2066 decrements before it tests.
Reads voice 2's next note, a pair of bytes at $92/$93, the same as $2075 for voice 1 but with no end marker: voice 2 runs on until voice 1 restarts the tune.
Closes the gate of a voice, keeping pulse waveform: $40 to $D400 + X, which is $D404 for voice 1 (X = 4) and $D40B for voice 2 (X = $0B).

Pitch 0 of the in-game tune's note table, $20EC-$21AB: 96 little-endian SID frequency words, read at $208E and $20C7 by twice the pitch. Pitch 0 is a rest, so this word is never read. The table is the one the title uses at $A207, value for value.
High byte $00 of the first little-endian word at $20EC (JSW_State_game_note_frequency_table); the parent description defines the table or writable pointer.

Pitches 1-95 of the note table at $20EC: by the NTSC clock (1,022,727 Hz) they run from C#0 ($011C) to B7 ($FD2E) a semitone apart, pitch 58 being $1DDF, A#4 at 466.2 Hz. Pitch 79, 25271, is the exception, 30.6 cents flat of G6; the low pitches are within 6 cents. On a PAL machine (985,248 Hz) every note is 65 cents lower than on NTSC, pitch 58 at 449.1 Hz.
Frame 0 of the spare life's four, $21AC-$222B, 32 bytes each: the four glyphs $3B-$3E that $3304 draws a spare life with, copied to $79D8 by the play interrupt every 15 frames while the music is on.
Frames 1-3 of the spare life at $21AC.
Code 0 of the four screen codes $35A7 draws map cells with: $20, air.
Codes 1-3 of the table at $222C: $21 floor, $22 wall, $23 hazard.
A bit-7 mask, read only by the ramp drawer: BIT $2230 at $2F65 tests offset $D3 of the room record (every floor a ramp) and at $2F80 offset $D5 (the ramp runs down to the left).

Mask 0, $01, the first of the eight bit masks $01 up to $80 at $2231-$2238, each picking out one sprite's bit. $300B reads them as $2231,X, X being the sprite, to switch on sprites 1 up; $3067 and $370D read them as $2232,Y and $2232,X, the index being the guardian's slot, to set the X high bit of its sprite, the slot plus one.
Second entry of the ascending bit-mask table, named because indexed references begin here.

Entries 2-7 ($04,$08,$10,$20,$40,$80) of the ascending bit-mask table $2231-$2238, followed by entry 0 ($FE) of its bitwise-inverted counterpart $2239-$2240. Indexed consumers use bases $2231/$2232 for setting bits and $223A for clearing them. Each inverted entry is $FF XOR the matching ascending mask; the final seven inverse entries are described at $223A.

Entries 1-7, $FD,$FB,$F7,$EF,$DF,$BF,$7F, of the descending inverted-mask table $2239-$2240 ($FE,$FD,$FB,$F7,$EF,$DF,$BF,$7F). $306F and $3715 read it as $223A,Y and $223A,X with the guardian's slot, to clear the X high bit of its sprite, the slot plus one.
32 C64 screen codes for the gameplay status-line template.
Per-digit ASCII rollover thresholds used by the six-digit clock incrementer.
Initial ASCII clock digits copied to $37-$3C, representing 07:00:00.

The first of the 19 pointers the play interrupt rotates right at $349D, a bit each frame, read from the last down. Each points at a row of a room's conveyor glyph in the room's own record at $B000 or $E000: offset $C0, its top row, or $C2, its third. $34CF then copies the current room's glyph to $25 at $7928. This one is The Off Licence's third row. With $2297, the tables give 17 conveyors their top row turning their way and their third row the other way. The Forgotten Abbey, The Nightmare Room, The Bathroom, Orangery, Tool Shed and The Beach have a pointer to their top row alone, turning their way, so their third row never turns. West of Kitchen also has only its top row, and it turns right though its conveyor carries Willy left. The conveyors of Ballroom West, Master Bedroom, Emergency Generator, Conservatory Roof and The Bow have no pointer, so their glyphs never turn.
Pointers 2-19 of the table at $2271.
The first of the 22 pointers the play interrupt rotates left at $34B8, a bit each frame: rows of conveyor glyphs in the room records, as at $2271. This one is The Bathroom's top row.
Pointers 2-22 of the table at $2297.

Item record 0 of the 80 at $22C3-$2402, four bytes each: room, column, row, and the taken flag, $FF once taken ($15FB). Taking an item adds one to the count at $0401, in decimal; at 50, $0400 is set and Maria leaves.
Item records 1-79 of the table at $22C3.

Arrow record 0 of the 16 at $2403-$2442, four bytes each: the room, with bit 7 set while the arrow flies; a countdown to its next flight; its column, with bit 7 set flying left; its row. $314D processes the first 15. Records 7, 11 and 12 ($241F, $242F, $2433) name room 99, which does not exist, so they never fly.
Arrow records 1-15 of the table at $2403. $314D's loop of 15 never reaches record 15, at $243F, in The Beach.

Guardian record 0 of the 181 at $2443-$29EA, eight bytes each: type (bit 7 going across, bit 6 the starting direction), column, row, base frame, upper bound, frame mask, speed and lower bound. A room's offsets $E0 and $E1 pick its first record and how many ($2FCD).
Guardian records 1-24 of the table at $2443, eight bytes each.

Entrance to Hades' fourth and last guardian, sprite 4: type $80, going across, at column $37 and row $19. Row $19 puts it at height $FA, the foot of the screen, below the room, and column $37 wraps round to x $F0. Its frame mask is 0, so $369E moves it right a cell an update and left a cell every four, through frames $2F down to $2C. The Chapel's last guardian, at $277B, is the same record.

The Chapel's seventh and last guardian, sprite 7: the same record as Entrance to Hades' at $250B, at height $FA, the foot of the screen, below the room, with frame mask 0 ($369E). The Chapel is not one of the rooms where $324E or $3284 take sprite 7 over.

Room 38 final guardian slot. Copied normally to work slot 4 and assigned to VIC sprite 5. Type $00 selects the vertical updater; row $19 maps to Y $FA and zero vertical-pixel step leaves it parked there, with only the direction bit toggling. Ordinary-format off-screen dummy.
Room 0's eight sprite colours, the first of 60 rows at $29EB-$2BCA: sprite 0, Willy, to sprite 7. $2FCD loads a room's row into $D027-$D02E when the room has guardians.
The sprite colours of rooms 1-59, eight a room, in the table at $29EB.
Row 0's pointer, $7C04, the first of the 16 at $2BCB-$2BEA: row r of the room starts at $7C04 + 40 r, column 4 of screen row r, and its colour RAM $5C00 higher.
High byte $7C of the first little-endian word at $2BCB (JSW_State_room_screen_row_pointers); the parent description defines the table or writable pointer.
Row pointers 1-15 of the table at $2BCB: row r of the room starts at $7C04 + 40 r, column 4 of screen row r.

Entry 0 of the 64-byte key table at $2BEB-$2C2A that the gameplay input scan reads at $37E8: for each key down, the entry at 8 times its keyboard row plus 7 minus its column gives the key's code. Entry 0 is $11, cursor down (row 0, column 7).
Entries 1-63 of the gameplay key table at $2BEB.

The first of the eleven left keys, Q E T U O @ 1 3 5 7 9, the first of four lists of eleven key codes: left from $2C2B, right from $2C36, jump from $2C41, pause from $2C4C. The loop at $380B compares each key down with the left, right and jump lists ($380B, $3814, $381D); the main loop compares the first key down with the pause list at $3120.
Left keys 2-11, E T U O @ 1 3 5 7 9, of the list at $2C2B.
Keyboard aliases accepted for movement to the right.
Keyboard aliases accepted for jump.
The eleven pause keys, A S D F G H J K L : ;, compared with the first key down by the main loop at $3120. Any key ends a pause and a pause key starts one, so a key off this list ends it.

Starts a game. It puts the video chip in bank 1 ($4000-$7FFF) with the screen at $7C00 and the character set at $7800, in extended colour mode; banks BASIC out ($01 = $36); stops the timer interrupt of CIA 1; clears zero page $07-$5F and the taken flag of all 80 items. Willy starts in The Bathroom (room 33) at column 20 and height $68, which is also the first checkpoint, with eight spare lives, the music on ($35) and the volume $5F at 12. The play interrupt $33E1 goes in at raster line $FB, $2005 sets up the tune, and the seven vectors at $CFF0 are written. The screen is cleared to $C0, rows 19-24 (from $7EF8) to $A0 in white, the clock set to 07:00:00 from $2267 and the status line from $2241. Then on into $2DC6 with the room build.
X=$00..$58 clears $07-$5F; $60 is outside the loop.

Places Willy in the room he has just entered, $0E, by which exit of the room he left ($1D-$20) names it, tested in the order up, down, right, left. Through the old room's top: at the bottom, height $68, falling (state 2) with the fall counter and the deadly-fall flag cleared. Through its bottom: at the top, height 0, falling, with the counter kept, so a fall goes on counting from room to room. Through its right side: column 0 at phase 4. Through its left side: column 30 at phase 4. An exit that leads back to the same room is matched by the first side that names it, so leaving such a room by its right side with its up exit also its own number puts Willy at the bottom. Then the room is built from $2E07.

The start of a room build: only Willy's sprite on, every sprite at x 0, sprites 1-7 parked at heights $10 to $D0, the raster compare set to line 0, and the sprite-sprite collision latch cleared by a read. On into $2E55.

Copies the room's 256-byte record to $0840-$093F: rooms 0-29 from $B000 + 256 times the room, rooms 30-59 from $E000 on. Rooms 30-59 sit under the KERNAL ROM, so the copy runs with interrupts off and $01 = $34, every bank RAM, and puts $36 back after. On into $2E7C.

Saves Willy's checkpoint, the eight fields the death sequence at $38EF puts back: his state ($33 to $57), height ($1C to $58), fall counter ($51 to $59), phase ($32 to $5A), cell ($4F to $5B), room ($0E to $5C), frame ($50 to $5D) and jump index ($52 to $5E). It runs on every room entry, so Willy restarts where he came in, in whatever state he came in: a fall that was already deadly is saved with its count. On into $2E9C.

Draws the room from its record at $0840. The border and background 3 take offset $D6; background 0 and the colour of air take $D7; floor, wall and hazard colours $D8-$DA go to $24-$26; the conveyor colour $DB to $15. Voice 3's frequency is cleared. The name, 32 characters, goes on row 17 from column 4 in white on background 2, a letter ($41 and up) taken down to its screen code. The map, 128 bytes from offset $20, is four cells a byte, each drawn by $35A7. The six glyphs at offsets $A0-$CF go to $7908, the glyphs $21-$26; the arrow divider $1A is set to 4; and the four exits at $DC-$DF are copied to $1D-$20. On into $2F28.

Draws the room's conveyor, when offset $D0 is not zero: its direction in $13 is 1 (right) or, with bit 7 set, $FF (left); its length is the low six bits; it starts at column $D2, row $D1, and runs right in glyph $25, the conveyor colour. A room without one leaves $13 at 0. On into $2F5A.

Draws the room's ramp. With bit 7 of offset $D3 set no ramp is drawn: $10 becomes $FF, so every floor cell of the room counts as a ramp ($35E4), going the way of offset $D4. Otherwise, when offset $D5 is not zero, the ramp starts at column $D4, row $D3, and runs its low six bits of cells in glyph $24, the colour of hazards ($26), down and to the right (40 + 1 a step) or, with bit 7 set, down and to the left (40 - 1). Its direction goes to $11, 1 or $FF. Bit 6 sets $12, which nothing reads. On into $2FCD.

Loads the room's guardians: offset $E1 of them, from the record at $2443 + 8 times offset $E0, to $0940. Each becomes sprite 1 up, switched on, with its starting direction in $0980 (bit 6 of its type), its column (byte 1) in $0988, which only a horizontal guardian moves, its frame from byte 3 and its place from bytes 1 and 2, a cell being 8 pixels from $38 across and $32 down. Then the room's eight sprite colours, from $29EB + 8 times the room, go to $D027-$D02E, and the vertical stretch of every sprite ($D017) is cleared. A room with no guardians skips all of this, colours too, and goes straight to $30A8.

Sets the rope up, in a room with one (offset $E2, copied to $0402): sprites 5-7 stretched tall ($D017 = $E0) with frames $AC-$AE, the swing at position 16, half 1, direction and step $FF. The sprite-background collision latch is cleared by a read. On into $30D9.
Reads the sprite-sprite collision latch $D01E 256 times, to clear it before play. On into $30E1.

In room 32, Halfway up the East Wall, puts six conveyor cells (glyph $25) into the room after it is drawn, one a row down and to the right from $7C5A, at screen addresses the code names, and sets the conveyor's direction $13 to 1, right. The six cells are the room's ramp (offsets $D3-$D5: row 2, column 6, six cells down to the right), which $2FA8 drew as glyph $24; their colour stays as the ramp drawing left it, $26, the room's offset $DA colour. On into the main loop at $30FF.

The main loop. Each pass waits a little ($33D0). While the game is paused ($36) the volume is turned off and the keys read with interrupts off, and the pass loops until a key is down. A key down ends a pause; a pause key (one of the eleven at $2C4C) starts one. Then on through $3132.
Ends the game when the first key down has the code 3, through $383B. On through $313F.
Calls the item routine $3983 on every pass, which draws the items only on every eighteenth pass ($55); then, on every eighth pass ($1A), moves the arrows at $314D. Either way on to $324E.

Goes through the first 15 arrow records. A record whose room, its first byte less bit 7, is not the current room is passed over untouched ($315D). For one that is, it counts the record's second byte down: at 10 a noise starts on voice 3 as a warning, and at 0 the sound stops and the arrow fires, with bit 7 of the first byte set and sprite 6 switched on. A flying arrow moves a column at a time and is shown as sprite 6 ($AA or $AB, by its direction) until it reaches the room's edge. Then sprite 6 is moved to height 0, the column byte is set to 0 (an arrow flying right) or $9F (column 31, flying left), bit 7 of the first byte is cleared and the record waits again. Only an arrow flying right also switches sprite 6 off ($31DE); one flying left leaves it on, at height 0. The loop stops after 15, so record 16 at $243F, in The Beach, never fires. Clobbers A, X, Y and arrow state.
Places sprite 6 as an arrow: A is the frame, $AA flying right or $AB flying left; X is the column and Y the row, a cell being 8 pixels from $38 across and $32 down.

In The Bathroom (room 33), shows the toilet as sprite 7: switched on, white, at x $118, height $9A, with the pass counter $1B going up by one and its bit 4 choosing frame $0E or $0F, so the frame changes every 16 passes. The toilet's other frames, $10 and $11, are never shown. Elsewhere on to $3284.

In the Master Bedroom (room 35), until Maria has gone ($0400), shows her as sprite 7, yellow, at x $A8, height $8A, and switches every other sprite off but Willy's ($D015 = $81). Her frame follows Willy's row, his height $1C divided by 8: from row 13 down, $02 and $03 by turns as bit 3 of the pass counter $1B changes; at row 12, $04; above it, $05. On to $32D4.

Moves the guardians on every twelfth pass ($3E): each of the $2D in the room, by $369E when bit 7 of its type is set (across) and by $3614 when it is clear (up and down), with its record offset in $2E and its number in $2F.

Draws the spare lives on the status line: one block of four glyphs, $7B $7D over $7C $7E, for each of the $41 spare lives, three columns apart from $7F70, the first in colour 1 and each one after in the next colour. None when the count is 0.
Runs the player update on every sixth pass ($56): the item count $0401 is kept in $0408 first, and $3349 starts the update. Other passes go straight to the collisions at $3392.
Resets the stack and starts a player update at $1000. The vector at $CFF2 points here, so a state handler can start the update again after changing the state, with nothing left on the stack.

Where a player update ends when it neither changes room nor kills Willy, through the vector at $CFF4 ($1021); an update that changes room goes on to $2DC6 through $1027, and a death to $38EF through $102A. The stack is reset, and when the item count has changed during the update, the pick-up sound plays: voice 3, pulse, its frequency swept up one step at a time to $2500 in a loop the game waits for, then the gate closed. The sweep starts at $20xx: the high byte $08 is set to $20, and the low byte $07 is left as the update left it. On to $3392.

Kills Willy when the sprite-sprite collision latch $D01E has his bit set. In The Bathroom a touch that includes sprite 7, the toilet, is safe. In a room with a rope only sprites 1-4 kill, sprites 5-7 being the rope; in any other room anything he touches kills him, Maria and the arrow included. The death is $38EF. On to $33BB.
Ends the game when the clock's hours read 12 ($37 and $38 are "1" and "2"), through $383B; otherwise back to the top of the main loop.
A pause of about 3,800 cycles: X counts down from 256 three times. The main loop's pace.
The end of the play interrupt: Y, X and A taken back off the stack, which the KERNAL's entry pushed, and RTI.

The play interrupt, from the raster at two lines a frame. While the game is paused it does nothing. At line 0 it goes to $3594, which reads the keys. At line $FB it sets the next interrupt for line 0 and runs the frame. The music: when it is off ($35), voices 1 and 2 are gated off and their frequencies cleared; when it is on, every second frame $2066 ticks three times. The clock: every 50 frames a second goes on, the digits rolling over at the limits at $2261, and the time is printed at $7F40 as HH:MM:SS. The conveyors: with $01 = $34 the IRQ rotates 41 bytes of conveyor glyphs in the room records themselves, at offsets $C0 and $C2 of 24 rooms, 19 a pixel to the right from the pointers at $2271 and 22 to the left from $2297. Five rooms that have a conveyor (21, 35, 39, 43 and 59) have no pointer, so their conveyor never moves. It then copies the current room's conveyor glyph (offsets $C0-$C7) to glyph $25 at $7928. Every 15 frames, while the music is on: + ($2B) raises the volume in $5F and - ($2D) lowers it, within 0 to 15, it goes to $D418, and the spare-life glyphs $3B-$3E at $79D8 take the next of four frames from $21AC, so the spare lives stand still while the music is off. In a room with a rope ($0402), when $0407 is 0, the rope's staged sprites and places are copied to $6B00 and $D00A, and $0407 is set to $FF. Last, Willy's sprite: x from his cell, 8 pixels a cell from $38; y his height plus $32; and his frame $50 his facing (bit 2) plus half his phase, shown as sprite frame $50 + 6. A pause check at $340A never passes, because a paused game left at $33EE.
The line-0 half of the play interrupt: sets the next interrupt for line $FB, reads the keys and the joystick ($3791) and leaves through $33DB.

Draws one cell of the room map at $2E9C: its 2-bit value picks the screen code from $222C ($20 air, $21 floor, $22 wall, $23 hazard) and the colour from $23-$26, written at row $62 and column $61 through the row pointers at $2BCB, with the colour RAM address $5C00 above the screen's. The column then moves on, to the next row after 32. It returns the map byte, kept in $0C, in A for the next cell.

The tile lookup, also reached through $1024: the kind of tile at column X and row Y of the room, in A. It points $07/$08 at the cell's screen address, from the row pointers at $2BCB, and $09/$0A at its colour RAM, $5C00 above, and returns the screen code's low five bits: 0 air, 1 floor, 2 wall, 3 hazard, 4 ramp, 5 conveyor, 6 item. Floor reads as ramp when $10 is set, in a room where every floor is a ramp. Y is 0 on return.

Moves a guardian that goes up and down, by its record at $0940 + X and its state at $0980 + its number: bit 7 of the state set means going up. Each move is byte 6 of the record, in pixels. Going down it turns, without moving, when the row of the new height would reach byte 4; going up, when it would be above byte 7 or past row 14. A move also steps the frame: the state's count, up one going down and down one going up, masked by byte 5 and by 3, is added to the base frame, byte 3.

Moves a guardian that goes across, by its record at $0940 + X, its state at $0980 + its number (bit 7 set means going left) and its column at $0988 + its number. Going right, the count in the state goes up, and the frame is the base frame (byte 3) plus the count, plus 4 when byte 5 is 4 or more; when the count passes byte 5's low two bits it goes back to 0 and the guardian moves a cell right, turning instead when the column reaches byte 4. Going left, the count goes down from 3, whatever the mask, with frames the base plus the count and never the 4 more; below 0 the guardian moves a cell left, turning instead below byte 7 or below 0. So a guardian whose mask is below 3 goes left more slowly than right, through frames it never shows going right; two records have mask 0, $250B and $277B, both parked at height $FA, below the room.

Reads joystick port 2 and the keyboard into the signed direction $49 ($FF left, $01 right, $00 neither) and the jump request $4A. The reversal test at $382C never passes, because $60 is never set (see $0060), so it always leaves $4B at $00. Clobbers A, X and Y; the joystick's bits 2, 3 and 4 are left, right and fire, active low.
From unseeded $60=$00 and $49 in {$00,$FF,$01}, A cannot equal $FE; branch body is unreachable on this route.

Game over, from the clock ($33BB), the last life ($397D) or RUN/STOP ($313C). The sound and the sprites go off and the pause flag $36 is set, which stops the play interrupt. The room's 32 by 16 cells are wiped a column at a time to spaces in colour 0, the border taking the column's number as it goes. The background ($D021) keeps the room's colour, so the wiped room is black in 50 rooms and coloured in ten, yellow in Entrance to Hades (room 6). Then the boot (sprite 0, frame $00) drops from the top of the screen at x $B0, the border flashing with its height, onto Willy (sprite 1, frame $08) standing on the barrel (sprite 2, frame $01). When it reaches height $92, Willy takes the background's colour, and after a wait ($38D8) the title starts again at $A000.
A long wait for game over: $38E3 20 times, and once more as it falls into it.
A wait of 16 times $33D0.

The death sequence, reached through the vector at $CFFA ($102A, from the player code at $15F6) and by direct jumps from the sprite-collision check at $33A7, $33AF and $33B8. The sprites go off and the border goes white while voice 3 plays noise at full volume, its frequency swept from $0200 up to $11FF in a loop the game waits for; then the volume goes back to $5F and the border to its colour. Willy's checkpoint, saved at $2E7C on entering the room, is put back, the spare-life rows of the status line are cleared, and a life is taken from $41. Below zero the game is over ($383B); otherwise the room is built again from $2E07, with Willy where he came in.

Draws the items not yet taken on every eighteenth pass ($55): each of the 80 records at $22C3 for this room ($0E) with byte 3 still 0 is drawn as glyph $26 at its column and row, in colour $19. $19 goes up by one before the pass and after every record, so the items' colours change each time. On into $39F1.
Turns the in-game music off and on ($35) when the first key down is Return. It runs only after an item pass ($3983), so Return is read every eighteenth pass.

The code card, run by the original loader once the game had loaded; in this BCS release nothing calls it. Copies the failure header to $8000 ($3C77), clears the screen, sets up voice 3, prints LOADING COMPLETE... PRESS A KEY TO START ($3C8F) and waits for a key, then asks for the code at $3B20.
Waits until the keyboard scan at $3791 reports a key in $43. The scan runs with interrupts off; CLI comes before the RTS.

The base address of the code card's answers, $2C57: the start of the game's own initialiser. $3B65 adds four times the cell number to it and reads four bytes from there, keeping the low two bits of each as a colour. So the answers are the game's own code: 360 cells of four colours, from the 1,440 bytes $2C57-$31F6.
The high byte of the answer base at $3A61, $2C.

X and Y for sprites 0 to 3, the four colour slots, at X $38, $58, $78 and $98, Y $80: $3BC1 copies these eight bytes to $D000-$D007. The two bytes after them, $38 and $98 at $3A6B-$3A6C, are never read. The cursor, sprite 4, is placed by $3C15, at the X of the slot being entered ($3A63 plus twice the slot), and $3C1B, at Y $9C.
The slot being entered, 0 to 3. $3C08 adds one and masks it with 3, so the cursor wraps from the fourth slot to the first.
Eight sprite colours: red, green, blue and yellow for sprites 0 to 3, the same again for 4 to 7. Pressing 1 to 4 colours the current slot with the first four.
Zero on the first try. A wrong code sets it and asks again for a new cell; a second wrong code goes to the red screen at $3C6B.

The four colours entered, 0 to 3 for keys 1 to 4, $FF for an empty slot. $3C23 sends a code back while any slot is empty, then compares all four with $3A81-$3A84. Only slot 0 is emptied when a code is asked for ($3B23), so the other three keep what they held. In this file all four are spaces ($20), as are the four at $3A81: no code was asked for before the file was saved, because $3B20, which fills $3A81, never ran. The failure header at $8000, which only $3C77 writes, suggests that the card's start at $3A02 had run.
The four colours the card holds for the chosen cell, from the low two bits of four bytes of the game's code (see $3A61).
The limit the random-number routine at $3B12 is working to: 20 for the row, 18 for the column.
The row of the cell asked for, 0 to 19. $3B3D reads its offset from $3AE8 and $3BA8 its label from $3AC0.
The column asked for, 0 to 17. $3B9E prints it as column plus 1, which the screen shows as a letter, A to R.
"ENTER CODE AT GRID LOCATION", 28 characters, printed at $042E-$0449 on the first try.
"SORRY,TRY AGAIN AT LOCATION", 28 characters, printed in the same place after a wrong code.
The row labels "0 " to "19", two characters each, printed after the column letter at $044B-$044C.
Second-byte operand base for the 20 two-character row labels at $3AC0-$3AE7. $3BAE reads this base plus twice the selected row and writes the right-hand displayed character.
Twenty little-endian words, 18 times the row: the number of the first cell in each row of the card.

High-byte operand base for the 20 little-endian row offsets at $3AE8-$3B0F. $3B42 reads this base plus twice the chosen row. The following two bytes at $3B10-$3B11 are outside the indexed table and their meaning is open.
A twenty-first row offset, $0168 (20 times 18). The row is always below 20, so it is never read.
Picks a random number below A: reads SID voice 3's oscillator, keeps five bits and tries again while the result is A or more. Called with 20 for the row and 18 for the column.

Asks for a code: waits for the keys to be released ($3CC9), empties slot 0 of the four (X is 0 after $3CC9, so the loop at $3B25 stores once), picks a random row and column, reads the four answers from the game's code (see $3A61), prints the prompt with the cell's column letter and row number, and shows the four slot sprites and the cursor. Then polls for keys 1 to 4 and Return.
Takes one key: Return checks the code at $3C23; 1 to 4 store 0 to 3 in the current slot and change its sprite to that keycap in that colour. Other keys are ignored.
Waits until no key is held, moves on to the next slot (wrapping after the fourth) and moves the cursor. Return with a slot still empty also comes here.
Checks the code: an empty slot ($FF, bit 7 set) sends it back to $3C00; otherwise it compares the four slots with the four answers, last first. A match goes to $3C3A, any difference to $3C4E.

A correct code: copies the success header to $8000 ($3C83), waits for the keys to be released, clears $43-$47 (the key count, the three decoded keys and the scan's bit index $47) and jumps to $0FA0 with interrupts off, which starts the title.
A wrong code: the first time sets the retry flag and asks again at $3B20; the second time goes to the red screen at $3C6B.
Nine bytes, a cartridge header: both start vectors $3C6B, then CBM80. $3C77 copies it to $8000, so that RESTORE or a reset during the code card ends on the red screen.

Nine bytes, a cartridge header: both start vectors $0FA0, then CBM80. $3C83 copies it to $8000 after a correct code, so that RESTORE goes back to the title. A reset would not: it leaves the processor port's direction register $00 at 0, so $0FA0's write to $01 changes nothing, BASIC ROM stays in, and the jump to $A000 runs into it and jams the processor at $A005.
The end of a second wrong code: interrupts off, border and background red, and a loop to itself.
Copies the failure header, $3C59-$3C61, to $8000-$8008.
Copies the success header, $3C62-$3C6A, to $8000-$8008.
"LOADING COMPLETE... PRESS A KEY TO START", 40 characters, ASCII. $3CB7 prints it on the top row.
Prints the message at $3C8F on the top row of the screen at $0400, turning its letters into screen codes with AND #$1F.
Calls the keyboard scan at $3791 until no key is down ($43 is 0), then turns interrupts back on.

A copy routine nothing calls: with the processor port at $36 it copies 32 pages, $B000-$CFFF, to $2000-$3FFF, then sets the port to $37. It sits inside its own destination: run where it is, the last page it copies ($CF00 onto $3F00) overwrites it as it runs, which works only if that page holds these same bytes. Its branches are all relative, so it would also run from a copy elsewhere. Whether and where it ran is not known.

Entry to the title screen: a jump to the initialiser at $A744. The BCS start-up stub at $080D jumps here once the file has loaded (from $081B), and the game jumps here again when a game ends (from $38D5). The code card's restart stub at $0FA0 also jumps here (from $0FA6), but this release never runs the code card.

Eight bytes, one per keyboard row: the title's scan at $A083 stores each row it reads from CIA 1 port B here, $A003 for the row with PA0 low up to $A00A for PA7. In the file as loaded, $A003 holds $FD, Return down in the last scan before the game's memory was saved; the first scan on the title screen replaces it with $FF when no key in that row is down. With no key held, it is the only byte of the listing that the title changes; the title also rewrites the screen at $7C00-$7FFF, zero page and the interrupt vector at $0314, which the listing leaves out.
Rows two to eight of the title's keyboard scan buffer (see $A003).
Fifty-six spaces between the title's scan buffer and its key table. Nothing reads or writes them.

The title's keyboard table, 64 PETSCII codes in matrix order: row (PA0 to PA7) times eight plus column, column 7 first. $A043 is CRSR down, $A049 is Return ($0D), $A04B to $A052 are LEFT SHIFT ($00), E, S, Z, 4, A, W, 3. The scan at $A083 reads it with LDA $A043,Y.
The rest of the title's 64-byte key table that starts at $A043, in the same row-and-column order. The title only acts on Return ($0D, at $A049).

Scans the keyboard for the title, from the raster-0 interrupt. Selects each row of CIA 1 in turn (PA0 first), storing what port B returns in $A003-$A00A, then looks through the rows for the first key that is down and turns it into PETSCII through the table at $A043. On return $50 is 0 when no key is down, or 1 with the key's code in $51; it stops at the first key it finds. Leaves $DC00 = $7F.

Starts the title tune from the top: points voice 1 at $6C00, voice 2 at $7248 and voice 3 at $7350 (through $0A/$0B, $0C/$0D and $0E/$0F), clears the SID, gives all three voices attack 0 decay 8, sustain 9 release 0, pulse widths of $258, $26C and $280 (about 15 %) and the pulse waveform gated on, sets volume 10 with no filter, clears the end flag $FE and sets each voice's countdown to 1 so that the first tick reads the first note.

One tick of the title tune: counts down each voice's duration ($4C, $4D, $4E) and reads that voice's next note when it reaches zero. The raster-0 interrupt calls it three times every second frame, so the tune runs at 75 ticks a second on a PAL machine.

Reads voice 1's next note, two bytes at ($0A): a pitch (0 for a rest, otherwise an index into the note table at $A207) and a duration in ticks (0 counts as 256). A duration of $FF ends the tune: it sets $FE to $FF, clears the SID and drops the return address to $A139, so the caller's other two voices are not read on that tick. The title loop at $A7F5 sees $FE and starts the tune again.
Reads voice 2's next note, pitch then duration, from ($0C) into the SID's voice 2 and $4D. Voice 2 has no end marker: voice 1's ends the tune for all three.
Reads voice 3's next note, pitch then duration, from ($0E) into the SID's voice 3 and $4E. Like voice 2, it relies on voice 1 to end the tune.

A rest in the title tune: zeroes the frequency of the voice whose registers start at $D400+X (X is 0, 7 or 14) and writes $40 to its control register, which leaves the pulse waveform selected with the gate off.

The title tune's note table: 96 little-endian SID frequency words, $A207-$A2C6, the same values as the in-game table at $20EC. Index 0 is never played (pitch 0 means a rest). Indexes 1 to 95 run from C#0 ($011C) to B7 ($FD2E) by the NTSC clock, a semitone apart except around index 79, 25271, which is 30.6 cents flat of G6. Index 58, $1DDF, is A#4 at 466.2 Hz on NTSC and 449.1 Hz on PAL: on a PAL machine every note is 65 cents lower than on NTSC.
The high bytes of the title note table at $A207, read as $A208,X by the three voice readers.
Notes 1 to 95 of the title note table that starts at $A207.

The scrolling message on the title screen, ASCII, from here to $A71B, followed by the 40 spaces at $A71C. In this BCS crack everything up to $A67F is the crackers' text ("BERLIN 16.10.1984: ... JET SET WILLY CRACKED BY THE BERLIN - CRACKING - SERVICE", greetings, and a jibe at Software Projects' colour code card); the game's own instruction follows at $A680. The ticker shows 40 characters starting one past the pointer, so this first byte is never on screen.
The BCS crackers' part of the title message, $A2C8-$A67F, which replaced whatever the original carried before the instructions at $A680. What that was is not in this image.
The end of the title message: "...MIDNIGHT SO THAT MARIA WILL LET HIM GO TO BED.........PRESS RETURN TO PLAY THE GAME...". The game's own text runs from $A680 to $A71B.
Forty spaces after the title message. When the pointer at $FB/$FC reaches $A71C the last window shown is these spaces, so the line is blank before the message starts again from $A2C7.

Sets up the title screen and starts its interrupt. Puts the video chip in bank 1 ($4000-$7FFF) through CIA 2, with the screen at $7C00 and the character set at $7800, and turns extended colour mode off; clears the screen and draws the logo ($A8AA), makes the border and background black and the ticker row (row 23) white, starts the title tune ($A0CD), points the ticker at $A2C7, stops CIA 1's timer A, turns the sprites off and installs the raster interrupt at $A801, first at line $EA. Falls into the title loop.

The title loop. Recolours the logo ($A88F) and waits for a key. Return starts the game: it sets $D011 = $5B (extended colour mode, 25 rows) and $D016 = 8, and jumps to $2000. Fire on joystick port 2 starts it too, but only while another key is down, because the loop reads the stick only when the keyboard scan found a key. When the title tune ends ($FE set) it starts the tune again.

The title's raster interrupt, which runs twice a frame. At line 0 it sets the next interrupt for line $EA (234), clears the fine scroll for the top of the screen, advances the tune three ticks every second frame (counting with $4F), restarts the message when its pointer reaches $A71C, and scans the keyboard ($A083). At line 234, just above the ticker row, it sets the next interrupt for line 0 and counts $4B down: the fine scroll is set to $4B, and when $4B reaches 0 the pointer moves on one character and the next 40 characters are copied to row 23 ($7F98), letters turned into screen codes with AND #$1F. One character every 8 frames. Both halves leave through the KERNAL's $FEBC, which restores the registers.

Colours the first 768 cells of the screen ($D800-$DAFF: rows 0 to 18 and the first eight cells of row 19, which take in the logo on rows 6 to 16) with one of the two colours at $A8A8, chosen by bit 2 of the ticker pointer's low byte. The logo therefore changes between red and green every four characters of the message, about every 32 frames. The rest of row 19 and rows 20 to 22, which hold only spaces, are not coloured.
The logo's first colour, red (2).
The logo's second colour, green (5).

Fills the screen at $7C00-$7FFF with spaces, prints PETSCII $08 through the KERNAL (which stops Shift and Commodore from switching the character set) and copies the title logo: 432 bytes from $A8D9 to $7CF0-$7E9F, screen rows 6 to 16.
The title logo, "JET SET WILLY" drawn in PETSCII line characters: 432 screen codes, 40 to a row, copied to rows 6 to 16 of the screen by $A8AA.
More of the title logo that starts at $A8D9.
The logo's second page, 176 bytes to $AA88, copied to $7DF0 by the second loop of $A8AA.
Writes zero to all 25 SID registers, $D400-$D418, which silences every voice and sets the volume to 0.

Bytes nothing in the game reads, $AA95-$AFFF: mostly the alternating $FF and $00 a C64's memory holds at power-on, saved into the file with the game. The routine at $AB80, which nothing calls, sits in the middle of it.

A copy routine nothing calls: copies sixteen pages, $C000-$CFFF, to $A000-$AFFF, with its pointers in $50-$53. A conveyor of 12 cells at row 9, column 19, moving left. A ramp of 4 cells from row 11, column 26, running down to the left. 12 items.
